articles.title: It's Time to End Qualified Immunity
articles.dek: A court-created doctrine often prevents people from holding government officials accountable for constitutional violations. Here’s how qualified immunity works, why it remains controversial and where reform efforts stand.
articles.author: The Ocmulgee Free Press
articles.featuredImageAlt: Two uniformed police officers stand outdoors. One officer, wearing sunglasses, holds a wooden baton across his body, while the other stands beside him with a hand resting near his duty belt.
articles.featuredImageCaption: Photo by Kindel Media on Pexels
body: When a government official violates your constitutional rights, you should be able to hold them accountable in court. In practice, a legal doctrine called qualified immunity often makes that nearly impossible. It's time for Congress and the states to end it.
## What Qualified Immunity Is

Qualified immunity is a court-created defense that shields government officials — most often police officers — from being personally sued for violating someone's constitutional rights. It emerged from a series of Supreme Court decisions and was substantially expanded in the 1982 case Harlow v. Fitzgerald.

Under the doctrine, a victim can only win a civil rights lawsuit against an official if the official violated a “clearly established” right — meaning a prior court case, with nearly identical facts, already ruled that specific conduct unconstitutional. If no case exactly on point exists, the official walks away immune, even if what they did was plainly wrong.

That standard has proven almost impossible to meet. Courts have granted immunity in cases involving officers who stole property while executing a search warrant, released a police dog on a suspect who had already surrendered, and shot a child while aiming at a nonthreatening family dog — all because no earlier case matched the facts closely enough.
## Why It Matters Right Now

Qualified immunity isn't an abstract legal debate — it continues to shape real cases in 2026. In March, the Supreme Court granted qualified immunity to a Vermont police officer sued by a nonviolent protester injured during a sit-in at the state capitol, over a dissent from three justices. That same term, the Court also declined to disturb a Seventh Circuit ruling shielding correctional officers who pepper-sprayed an inmate with a known medical contraindication and left him naked in a cold cell for 23 hours — again over a sharp dissent from Justice Sotomayor, who called the immunity grant “clearly wrong.”

These aren't outliers. They reflect how the “clearly established law” test operates: it asks not whether conduct was wrong, but whether some earlier court happened to say so under nearly identical circumstances. Justice Clarence Thomas — no liberal on this issue — has himself expressed “strong doubts” about the doctrine's legitimacy, noting that it lacks grounding in the text of the statute it purports to interpret, 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
## The Case for Ending It

It denies victims their day in court. Section 1983, the Reconstruction-era law meant to let people sue officials who violate their rights, contains no mention of qualified immunity. The Supreme Court invented the defense decades after the statute was passed, and it now regularly forecloses meritorious claims before a jury ever hears them.

It undermines accountability. When officials know they're personally shielded from liability except in the narrowest circumstances, the deterrent effect of civil rights law weakens. Departments and individual officers face less pressure to correct misconduct.

It's inconsistently and arbitrarily applied. Because the doctrine hinges on finding a nearly identical prior case, outcomes often turn on happenstance — whether some other plaintiff, in some other circuit, previously sued over comparable conduct — rather than on the merits of what happened to the person in front of the court.

It has drawn opposition across the political spectrum. Reform efforts have brought together civil rights organizations like the ACLU and NAACP with libertarian and conservative groups like the Cato Institute and the Institute for Justice, who see the doctrine as inconsistent with limited-government and rule-of-law principles.
## Where Reform Stands Today
Momentum has been building, though federal action remains stalled:

- Congress: Several bills are pending in the current session, including the Qualified Immunity Abolition Act of 2026 (S. 3625 / H.R. 7046), introduced by Senator Ed Markey, which would eliminate the qualified immunity defense entirely for claims under Section 1983. A revived version of the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act would end the doctrine for law enforcement specifically. Neither has passed as of this writing. Competing legislation, including bills such as S. 122 and H.R. 503, would instead codify and strengthen qualified immunity — underscoring that this remains a live and contested legislative fight.

- The Supreme Court: The Court has repeatedly declined invitations to revisit or narrow the doctrine, including a batch of cert denials in past terms and its ruling this spring in Zorn v. Linton. Reform through the courts alone looks unlikely in the near term.

- The states: Several states have acted on their own. Colorado eliminated qualified immunity as a defense to state constitutional claims in 2020. New Mexico passed the New Mexico Civil Rights Act in 2021, creating a state-law cause of action free of the defense. New York has pending legislation (S. 176 / A. 1402) that would do the same. Because these are state-law fixes, they don't affect federal claims, but they show reform is achievable at the state level even while Congress is deadlocked.
## What You Can Do
Change here has come from sustained public pressure as much as from litigation, so if this issue matters to you, here's where to start:

- Contact your members of Congress and ask them to support ending qualified immunity — whether through the Qualified Immunity Abolition Act, the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act, or similar legislation. Find your representatives at [congress.gov/members](https://www.congress.gov/members) and track bill status at [congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov).

- Push for state-level reform. If your state hasn't acted, state legislators can create a state-law cause of action that bypasses federal qualified immunity, as Colorado and New Mexico have done. Check your state legislature's website for pending bills.

- Support organizations working on this issue, including [ACLU](https://www.aclu.org), [Institute for Justice](https://ij.org), [NAACP Legal Defense Fund](https://www.naacpldf.org) and [Cato Institute](https://www.cato.org).

- Follow and share credible reporting on pending cases and legislation, including coverage from [SCOTUSblog](https://www.scotusblog.com) and the [Brennan Center for Justice](https://www.brennancenter.org).

- Vote and engage locally. Many police-accountability decisions — including union contracts, use-of-force policies and oversight boards — are made at the city and county level, where public pressure can be especially effective.

articles.title: Flock Safety’s Transparency Portal Is a Joke — And That May Be the Point
articles.dek: Flock Safety markets its Transparency Portal as public accountability, but incomplete search logs, corporate messaging and carefully framed FAQs make independent scrutiny nearly impossible.
articles.author: The Ocmulgee Free Press
articles.featuredImageAlt: Picture of a Flock Safety ALPR camera
body: Flock Safety would like the public to believe transparency is built into its surveillance network.

The company promotes its “Transparency Portal” as a way for communities to learn how local agencies use Flock’s automated license plate reader technology. On the surface, it sounds like exactly the sort of accountability tool that should accompany a surveillance system capable of recording the movements of millions of motorists.
Look a little closer, however, and the portal begins to resemble something else entirely: a carefully controlled public-relations exercise dressed up as transparency.

It offers glowing descriptions of the technology, statistics selected for public consumption, an FAQ that presents Flock’s version of controversial issues, and — in some cases — search logs stripped of information necessary to determine whether individual searches were actually legitimate.
Calling that “transparency” stretches the word beyond recognition.
## Transparency Without the Details
One of the most important accountability mechanisms offered through some Flock Transparency Portals is the publication of agency search activity.
That sounds promising.
If police are using a massive network of cameras to search motorists’ movements, the public should be able to examine how that power is being used.
But a meaningful audit requires context.
A useful search log should allow reviewers to answer basic questions:
- Who performed the search?
- Why was the search conducted?
- Was it connected to an actual investigation?
- Was a case number provided?
- What information was searched?
- When did the search occur?
Remove enough of those details and a “search log” becomes little more than a list of timestamps and vague explanations.
The public may technically be able to see that searches occurred while being given no realistic way to determine whether those searches complied with agency policy.
That isn't meaningful transparency. It is visibility without accountability.
Imagine a government credit-card report that showed the date of every purchase but concealed what was purchased, who made the purchase and where the money went.
Nobody would seriously call that a financial audit.

Yet Flock’s version of transparency can operate on essentially the same principle: show the public enough information to say the records are available, while withholding enough context to make independent scrutiny extraordinarily difficult.
## A Transparency Portal Written by the Company Being Scrutinized
There is another fundamental problem with the entire concept.
Flock Safety isn't an independent watchdog.
It is the company selling the surveillance system.
Yet much of the explanatory material appearing alongside these supposedly transparency-focused resources comes from Flock itself.
That creates an obvious conflict.

The company has every financial incentive to reassure residents that its technology is safe, effective, tightly controlled and respectful of privacy. Controversies surrounding automated license plate readers aren't merely abstract policy debates for Flock — they can influence whether cities renew contracts, whether lawmakers impose restrictions and whether communities accept additional cameras.
Visitors should therefore recognize the distinction between disclosure and marketing.
A page explaining why the company’s own product supposedly isn't a threat to privacy isn't independent transparency simply because the word “transparency” appears at the top.
It's corporate messaging.
## The FAQ Is Where Things Get Particularly Interesting
Flock’s FAQ sections attempt to answer many of the questions residents are increasingly asking about automated license plate readers.
- Who owns the data?
- Can agencies access cameras outside their jurisdiction?
- Does Flock track people?
- How long is information retained?
- Can federal agencies obtain access?
- What safeguards prevent abuse?
These are legitimate questions involving privacy, civil liberties and government surveillance.
They deserve precise answers.

Instead, corporate FAQs can rely on carefully framed statements that may be technically defensible in isolation while leaving out important context necessary for the public to understand how the network actually operates.
There is an enormous difference between answering a question and answering it completely.

For example, focusing exclusively on whether a camera uses facial recognition does little to address the broader privacy concern surrounding a system capable of recording where vehicles appear and allowing authorized users to search those observations.
Likewise, telling residents that agencies establish policies governing searches doesn't answer the obvious follow-up question:
Can the public actually verify that those policies are being followed?
If the search records made available for public review omit the information necessary to make that determination, the supposed safeguard becomes largely a matter of trust.
And “trust us” is not transparency.
## The Missing Information Matters
The omissions become especially troubling because abuse of surveillance technology does not necessarily look dramatic.
It can be one improper search.
An officer searching a former partner.
Someone looking up a neighbor.
A search performed for personal curiosity.
A plate queried without a legitimate law-enforcement purpose.
A search attributed to an investigation that doesn't actually exist.
Those are precisely the kinds of activities an audit should be capable of identifying.
But auditors need data.

If identifying information, search parameters, case references or meaningful justifications are absent, verifying suspicious activity can become substantially harder — sometimes impossible without obtaining the underlying records directly from the agency.
That raises an uncomfortable question:
What exactly is the transparency portal supposed to make transparent?

If residents must file open-records requests to obtain the information necessary to evaluate the activity displayed on the transparency website, then the website has failed at its most basic advertised purpose.
## Real Transparency Would Make Independent Verification Easy
There is nothing inherently complicated about meaningful transparency.

A genuinely useful public accountability system could provide appropriately redacted search logs containing enough information to determine whether searches correspond to legitimate law-enforcement activity.
It could publish agency policies prominently.
It could disclose what databases and external agencies are connected to the system.
It could provide historical statistics rather than selectively framed numbers.
It could explain documented limitations and controversies surrounding the technology rather than functioning primarily as a sales pitch.
Most importantly, it could provide enough information for journalists, researchers and ordinary residents to independently verify the claims being made.
Because transparency isn't measured by how much information an organization publishes.
It is measured by how much scrutiny that information permits.
## Transparency Shouldn't Require Trust
Flock Safety has built an extraordinarily powerful surveillance network.
That fact alone doesn't prove the technology is being abused. Automated license plate readers can unquestionably assist legitimate criminal investigations.
But powerful surveillance tools require powerful accountability mechanisms.
A company-operated webpage filled with reassuring explanations and incomplete records isn't an adequate substitute.

The public shouldn't have to accept Flock Safety’s description of its own technology at face value. Nor should residents have to assume every police search was legitimate simply because the information necessary to evaluate it has been omitted from the company’s transparency portal.
Accountability requires evidence.
Transparency requires context.
And oversight requires the ability to independently verify what government agencies — and the companies providing their surveillance infrastructure — tell us.
Without those things, Flock Safety’s Transparency Portal isn't really a window into the system.
It's a showroom window.
You can see exactly what the company wants you to see.

articles.title: Nearly Half of Bibb County Sheriff’s Flock Searches Had Recordkeeping Problems, Audit Finds
articles.dek: An independent forensic review of 3,663 Flock Safety searches found hundreds with no identifiable case number, widespread recordkeeping failures and high-volume bursts of plate lookups that auditors say warrant additional scrutiny.
articles.author: Ocmulgee Free Press Staff
body:
A forensic audit of the Bibb County Sheriff’s Office’s use of Flock Safety automated license plate reader technology has raised significant questions about how deputies and other personnel document their searches — and whether the agency can reliably demonstrate the investigative purpose behind every use of the surveillance system.

The audit examined 3,663 Flock Safety search-log entries generated by 63 user accounts between May 1 and June 1, 2026. Its central finding is striking: only 2,063 searches, or 56.3 percent, contained a properly formatted case or incident number in the designated “Case #” field. The other 1,600 searches — 43.7 percent of the total — either placed identifying information in the wrong field or contained no identifiable case reference at all.

The report does not conclude that those searches were unauthorized or that any individual employee intentionally misused Flock. In fact, the auditors explicitly caution against drawing that conclusion. What the findings expose instead is a significant accountability problem: when a powerful surveillance tool is used without consistent records tying searches to specific investigations, determining after the fact whether those searches were legitimate becomes considerably more difficult.

204 searches with no identifiable case

The most serious category identified by the audit consists of 204 searches — 5.6 percent of the entire dataset — for which investigators could identify no case or incident number anywhere in the record.

In those instances, the dedicated case-number field was blank and the reason field contained either no identifying number or only general descriptions such as “suspect,” “stolen,” “shooting” or “investigation.”

That distinction matters.

A search connected to a documented investigation can potentially be reviewed against an incident report, warrant, dispatch record or other agency documentation. A search recorded simply as “suspect” or “investigation” provides far less information to determine why a person or vehicle was queried.

The audit recommends that all 204 searches be individually reconciled against the agency’s records-management system to establish whether each was connected to a legitimate investigative purpose.

More than 1,300 searches documented incorrectly

Most of the questionable records do not appear to represent searches completely lacking a case reference. Instead, they reveal what the audit describes as a widespread recordkeeping problem.

Of the 3,663 searches examined, 1,396 — 38.1 percent — contained evidence that a case identifier had been entered incorrectly.

In 1,022 records, users apparently placed a case number in the free-text “Reason” field while leaving the designated case-number field blank. Another 347 records contained a Flock-generated “FID” identifier in place of an agency case number.

Because the same problem appears across numerous user accounts, the report suggests the pattern is more consistent with a systemic workflow or training problem than an isolated employee habit.

That explanation may be less alarming than intentional misuse, but it does not eliminate the accountability problem.

ALPR audit logs are supposed to make surveillance activity reviewable after it occurs. If investigators must manually reconstruct which case justified thousands of searches because identifying information was entered inconsistently, the usefulness of that audit trail is substantially weakened.

High-volume bursts deserve a closer look

The audit also identified 71 “burst sessions” in which the same user performed at least five plate lookups with no more than two minutes between consecutive searches.

Some were dramatically larger.

One user performed 128 lookups in approximately 14 minutes on May 30. Another performed 101 searches during a roughly 25-minute session. Other sessions included 59, 46 and 41 lookups.

Such activity is not inherently suspicious.

Investigators could legitimately run dozens of plates while working an organized theft investigation, searching for a wanted person or analyzing vehicles associated with a larger case. The report explicitly recognizes that possibility.

But several high-volume sessions lacked an agency case number entirely or relied on a Flock FID rather than an agency case identifier. That combination — unusually concentrated searching coupled with incomplete documentation — is why the auditors recommend supervisory review.

Among the sessions identified was a 41-lookup sequence lasting about 26 minutes with no case number entered. Another 33-lookups-in-12-minutes session also contained no case number. Additional sessions of 31, 26 and 25 searches likewise lacked an entered case number.

Without additional records, however, the audit cannot determine whether those searches represented legitimate investigative work or something else.

And that uncertainty leads to one of the report’s most important limitations.

Redactions prevent the most important verification

The data provided for analysis did not include the actual license plates searched.

According to the report, both the License and Filters fields were completely redacted from every row of the agency's export.

That means the auditors could determine when searches occurred, who conducted them and how closely together they were performed — but they could not determine whether a 40-search burst involved 40 different vehicles, repeated searches of one vehicle or some combination of the two.

The report therefore warns that its “repeated plate search” analysis is only a proxy based on temporal clustering rather than a direct comparison of license plates.

That limitation is particularly important when evaluating possible misuse. The existing records can identify activity that deserves further examination, but the redacted dataset cannot answer the ultimate question of what vehicles were actually being searched and why.

The audit recommends repeating the analysis using unredacted plate-level information if it can be made available through appropriate authorization.

A small group conducted most searches

Flock usage was also heavily concentrated among a relatively small number of accounts.

The median user performed just 13 searches during the audit period. The highest-volume account performed 553 searches — more than 42 times the median.

The top three accounts together generated 35.3 percent of all searches, while the top 10 accounted for roughly 70 percent of the agency’s entire search volume.

Again, volume alone is not evidence of misconduct. An investigator assigned specifically to vehicle-related cases or an intelligence analyst could reasonably use the system far more frequently than a patrol deputy.

The audit itself stresses that point, saying high-volume users should be viewed as a starting population for supervisory sampling rather than evidence of wrongdoing.

The concern becomes more significant when high search volume overlaps with missing case numbers, unusual search bursts or other documentation problems.
